description: We're a small team of Vietnamese computer science students with a research background in computer vision and geospatial data. We enjoy turning messy real-world data into something people can actually use, and we're excited to work hands-on with NASA open data this weekend

After the harvest, communes in An Giang, Vietnam, let the Mekong flood into their diked rice fields on purpose, then pump it out before sowing Winter–Spring rice; the sowing calendar closes on 31 December 2026. The commune's plan asks its People's Committee and cooperatives to track the flood for 24 hamlets, but gives them no map of where water still stands, and in the flood season the delta is often under cloud.

Flood Calendar uses NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar, which sees water through cloud, to keep a flood calendar for every 250 m block of Tân Hội commune (2,344 blocks, 14,650 ha). For each block it answers three questions: is water still there, when did it arrive, and how long has it stayed. Every date is a range between two radar passes. Across 22 radar passes, open water grew from 1,206 ha on 16 August to 9,850 ha by 3 November 2026, two-thirds of the area we mapped. The demo runs in two countries: An Giang, Vietnam, and Bang Rakam, Thailand. NISAR data are open and cover nearly all of Earth's land every 12 days, so the same steps can be repeated wherever flooded rice is grown.
details:
Why this matters now. After the harvest, communes in An Giang, Vietnam, let the Mekong flood into their diked rice fields on purpose. Then the water has to be pumped out before Winter–Spring rice can be sown, and the sowing calendar closes on 31 December 2026. Last season the flood receded slowly and sowing bunched together, the provincial agriculture department said. In April 2026 reporters found combine harvesters short in other An Giang communes, lodged rice waiting in the fields, and some farmers losing 500–700 VND per kilogram. The commune's plan asks it to track the flood, but gives it no map of the flood, and in the flood season the delta is often under cloud.

What we built. Flood Calendar reads NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar, which sees through cloud, and keeps a flood calendar for every 250 m block of Tân Hội commune: is open water still seen, when did it arrive, how long has it stayed. Across 22 radar passes, open water grew from 1,206 ha on 16 August to 9,850 ha by 3 November 2026, two days after the sowing calendar opened on 1 November. That is two-thirds of the 14,650 ha we mapped, a grid larger than the plan's 9,622 ha of diked fields. The flood is still at its widest, so the pumping-out phase is not in the record yet. So far the map marks 1,281 ha where open water is no longer seen, the first places a cooperative could check.

Where it goes next. The demo runs in two countries, on the same pipeline and web app: Tân Hội in An Giang, Vietnam, and Bang Rakam in Phitsanulok, Thailand. The second site needed its own site file, a threshold review and handling for mixed 10 m and 20 m pixels, and one of its three NISAR tracks gave no usable data. The target is every rice-growing country, 100+ of them: NISAR data are open and cover nearly all of Earth's land every 12 days, so the same steps can be repeated wherever flooded rice is grown.

The problem

Every autumn, Tân Hội commune in An Giang, Vietnam, opens the dikes around its rice fields after the Autumn–Winter harvest and lets the Mekong flood in. This is deliberate: the flood brings silt and cleans the fields between crops. Then the water has to be pumped out again before Winter–Spring rice can be sown, and the province's sowing calendar for that crop closes on 31 December 2026. A field that still holds water cannot be sown.

Last season showed what is at stake. The 2025 flood was high and receded slowly, so sowing in An Giang bunched together, the provincial Department of Agriculture and Environment said. In April 2026, reporters found the harvest bunched too. In An Giang communes such as Hòn Đất and Giồng Riềng, combine harvesters ran short, lodged rice waited in the fields, and some farmers lost 500–700 VND per kilogram on price as traders withdrew deposits (Báo Tin tức / Vietnam News Agency, 9 April 2026). A block-by-block view of where water still stands, refreshed every few days but about two weeks behind, could help a commune see uneven drainage before the calendar closes.

The commune's own plan sets out who has to make this work (Plan 122/KH-UBND, 12 May 2026, following provincial Letter 3767/SNNMT-KH). It covers 24 hamlets and 9,622 ha of diked fields:

- The Commune People's Committee sets the sowing window and the flood-release timing, and must update the flood level to adjust the sowing calendar.

- The flood-release zones pump the water out so they can sow within the calendar.

- The cooperatives track the water and announce the flood-release schedule to farmers.

Each of these duties needs the same answer: where is open water still standing, hamlet by hamlet, and since when? The plan asks the commune to track the flood; it does not give it a map of the flood. The season when the answer matters most is also the season when the delta is often under cloud, which limits optical satellites. Radar is not limited by cloud.

Reports give totals, not places. In the 2025 season, a provincial sowing report listed 25,053 of 505,712 ha (4.95%) of An Giang's planned Winter–Spring rice as sown (Official Letter 5395/SNNMT-CCTTBVTV). A number like that says how far the season has gone, not which fields still hold water.

Who it is for

- Commune People's Committee, Tân Hội. Decision: Sowing window and flood-release timing for 24 hamlets; when to adjust the calendar. What Flood Calendar gives them: For each 250 m block: is open water still seen, when it arrived, how long it has stayed. Summarised by nearest hamlet (hamlet names from OpenStreetMap).

- Agricultural cooperatives. Decision: Which areas to check first before announcing the schedule to farmers. What Flood Calendar gives them: Blocks where open water is no longer seen, and blocks where it is still seen, on the latest radar date. This does not mean a field is ready to sow.

- Later: provincial department. Decision: Progress across communes. What Flood Calendar gives them: The same view for other communes, after site set-up and a threshold review.

Flood Calendar does not replace a field visit. It shows where to send one.

NISAR data reaches us about two weeks after acquisition, so the map shows recent weeks, not today. Every date is a range between two radar passes.

These users and decisions come from the commune's published plan. We have not yet put the tool in front of commune staff; that is the next step.

Why NISAR

Flat open water reflects NISAR's L-band radar away from the satellite, so it shows dark in both HH and HV, with or without cloud, day or night. Tân Hội is covered by three NISAR tracks, so most blocks get a new look every 3–5 days, from free NASA data (one track misses about 14% of the blocks).

In our record, open water in Tân Hội grew from 1,206 ha on 16 August to 9,850 ha by 3 November 2026, the widest extent of the season so far, two days after the sowing calendar opened on 1 November. On the latest radar pass for each block, open water was still seen on 9,825 ha, had been there on every pass on 25 ha, and was no longer seen on 1,281 ha. These areas are within our 14,650 ha grid of 2,344 blocks, which is larger than the plan's 9,622 ha of diked fields. The 1,281 ha show where a cooperative could check first. The pumping-out phase is still ahead and is not in the data yet.

Radar mapping of flooded rice is established work: ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 inundation monitoring in An Giang (Hoang-Phi et al., 2026), multi-frequency SAR in Thai paddies (Kitratporn et al., 2026), the CH4Rice project, Arai et al. (2018) in the Mekong Delta, and NASA's OPERA DSWx-S1 surface-water product from C-band radar. What Flood Calendar adds is a calendar for each block (arrival range, days under water, current status) from NISAR's L-band, organised around the decisions in a commune's own plan, and told with a replayable map, sound and a 3D scene.

From two demo sites to 100+ rice-growing countries

The demo runs on two rice plains in two countries: Tân Hội in An Giang, Vietnam (2,344 blocks, 22 radar passes), and Bang Rakam in Phitsanulok, Thailand (2,304 blocks, 11 radar passes). Both use the same pipeline and the same web. Bang Rakam is a rice plain that Thailand's Royal Irrigation Department manages as a flood-retention area: its 2026 plan has farmers sow from 1 April and finish the harvest by mid-August so that the fields can take floodwater.

The target is global. Rice is grown in 100+ countries (117 rice-producing countries in the IRRI Rice Almanac, 4th edition), and NISAR images nearly all of Earth's land every 12 days, with open data. Wherever rice fields are flooded and NISAR passes over, the same three questions can be asked: is open water still seen, when did it arrive, how long has it stayed.

Adding a site takes three steps. Bang Rakam showed that each one is needed:

1. A site file: study area, NISAR tracks, grid and reference areas (config/sites/).

2. A threshold review for that site's images. Bang Rakam needed per-image thresholds and handling for mixed 10 m and 20 m pixels.

3. A comparison with a reference surface-water product where one exists. We used NASA OPERA DSWx-S1.

What it does

Flood Calendar uses NISAR L-band radar to answer three questions for every 250 m block of Tân Hội commune (2,344 blocks, 14,650 ha):

1. Is open water still there?

2. How long has the field been under water? Given as a minimum and a maximum number of days.

3. When did the water arrive? Given as a date range. On dry, flat fields the radar can mark the start earlier than it happened on the ground.

Each NISAR track revisits every 12 days, so every date is a range between two radar passes, never a single day.

The web app includes:

- A map that can be replayed radar pass by radar pass, and a chart for any single block.

- Data sound: tones follow the water area of each radar pass. The ambient landscape sound is illustrative.

- A 3D scene of each site with a narrated guided tour. The scene is an illustration (see Limits below).

- A layer for fields flooded more than 30 days before the season. The IPCC 2019 guidelines give such fields a higher methane scaling factor (Table 5.13). The layer only flags blocks, relevant if the IPCC default factor applies; it does not estimate emissions.

Bang Rakam (Thailand) has 2,304 blocks and 11 radar passes in a 12 × 12 km study frame, in the same web app.

What it does not do: it does not measure methane, and it cannot tell whether a field was sown right after the water left.

How it works

The pipeline runs offline and exports static files; the web app only reads those files.

- S0 Catalogue: Query NASA CMR for NISAR L2 GCOV scenes over the site; keep the latest processing version of each acquisition

- S1 Read: Read the HH and HV windows over HTTPS into a local cache

- S2 Grid: Prepare 250 m blocks and diagnostic HH/HV means

- S3 Reference: Measure a river reference and a stable area for each track; run three consistency checks

- S4 Classify: Apply HH/HV thresholds to pixels, require 75% water pixels, and filter single-image flips using a 50% fill guard

- S5 Indicators: Water arrival, days under water, current status, >30-day flag

- S6 Compare: Compare with OPERA DSWx-S1

- S7 Export: Write static files for the web

The export records default thresholds of HH < −14 dB and HV < −20 dB, with per-image overrides. It marks a block as water when at least 75% of jointly valid pixels meet both thresholds. A 50% threshold controls whether a single dry pass between two water passes is filled. The pixel method was selected after examining OPERA DSWx-S1 agreement; that agreement is post-hoc, not independent validation or field accuracy.

The file format between the pipeline and the web is defined in docs/data-contract.md (https://github.com/hungkhuu404/Dancing_with_The_Paddies/blob/main/docs/data-contract.md).

Limits

Final data (as published on 15 November 2026):

- Tân Hội: 22 NISAR acquisitions (radar passes) from tracks 047 D, 083 A and 148 D, 11 August–3 November 2026; 2,344 blocks (14,650 ha). Nine acquisitions use per-image thresholds instead of the default −14 dB HH / −20 dB HV.

- Bang Rakam: 11 acquisitions from tracks 011 A and 105 D, 14 August–31 October 2026; 2,304 blocks (14,400 ha) in a 12 × 12 km study frame, not an administrative boundary. Track 112 A images had no valid samples after the GCOV mask and are excluded. The 31 October 105 D image failed the stable-area check and uses per-image thresholds.

Limits:

- The 75% pixel method and 50% temporal guard were selected after examining OPERA DSWx-S1. Agreement with DSWx-S1 is post-hoc, not an independent test, and DSWx-S1 is not ground truth. The web does not report agreement scores.

- On the latest radar passes the flooded area was still at its largest. The record does not yet include the pumping-out phase that the tool is meant to follow; the next passes will show it.

- Sparse observations do not prove continuous flooding. One track revisits every 12 days, so water arrival, days under water and water leaving are ranges between two radar passes.

- The ">30 days" layer flags blocks, not verified continuous flooding. In Tân Hội it marks 8,093.75 ha as "yes"; in a post-hoc check the same rule applied to DSWx-S1 gave about 2,731 ha, so treat the layer as an upper bound.

- Trees and buildings can hide water from the radar; dry, flat fields can look like water, so water arrival may be dated early.

- Track 148 D misses about 14% of Tân Hội's blocks; the map uses each block's latest valid image.

- The 3D scene is an illustration: houses, people and vegetation are generated by rules, and roads, bridges and churches follow OpenStreetMap. It is not a surveyed model of the commune.

Team

Dancing with The Paddies, Ho Chi Minh City University of Technology (HCMUT), Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City (VNU-HCM): Khưu Huỳnh Gia Hưng (team lead, contact and submission); Lê Nguyễn Minh Tân, Lê Viễn Bằng and Lý Anh Quân (backend: radar pipeline and data); Phạm Anh Quốc and Lê Quang (frontend: web and video).

Tools: Python (NumPy, h5py, pyproj, Shapely), Vite, three.js, MapLibre GL JS; hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Code, data and full documentation: https://github.com/hungkhuu404/Dancing_with_The_Paddies
